To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the cleaning of hospital mattresses used in the treatment of patients with Candidemia is not sufficient to eliminate the fungal contamination of these mattresses.
the cleaning and disinfecting process of mattresses is not effective, since the mattresses are contaminated by Candida species.
(1) the cleaning and disinfecting process did not remove the fungi present on the mattresses and (2) there is a risk of these mattresses being potential reservoirs of infection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evaluation of the efficacy of the cleaning and disinfecting process of hospital mattresses.
the cleaning and disinfecting of mattresses used by patients suffering from candidemia in different hospital wards.
the contamination of hospital mattresses by fungi prior to and after cleaning and disinfecting them.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the study showed that 15 (60.0%) mattresses were contaminated by Candida sp, from these 10 (66,7%) and 5 (33,3%) corresponded respectively to collection before and after disinfection and that Candida parapsilosiss was the isolated species with highest frequency.
the results of the study show that 60% of the hospital mattresses used by Candidemia patients were contaminated by Candida species.
the cleaning and disinfecting process of hospital mattresses, as it was performed in this study, did not eliminate all the fungal contamination present in the mattresses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated the existence of fungal colonization in 60% of the mattresses prior to cleaning and disinfection and that 40% of the mattresses remained colonized after cleaning and disinfections.

the cleaning and disinfecting of mattresses used by patients infected with Candida spp. did not guarantee the removal of fungal contamination, and therefore there is a risk of these mattresses acting as potential secondary reservoir in the infection chain.
it is necessary to improve the quality of cleaning and disinfection of mattresses, as well as the training of nursing professionals to ensure the effectiveness of these procedures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cleaning of mattresses is not enough to remove all fungi.
the cleaning and disinfecting process of hospital mattresses is not sufficient to prevent the spread of fungal infections.
the use of a mattress with an antimicrobial coating is a viable alternative for preventing and controlling hospital acquired infections.
